article.title: On Clear Tasks and Meetings
article.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
article.content: by Jean Allen This essay is written in support of my convention resolution, For A Collectively Printed & Distributed Red Star . In it, I am motioning that we budget $3,600 for a printer and future printing costs through the year, and I understand that seems to be a lot. It will be compared to other front-facing work we have, other important committees, and people will ask why we should devote so much energy, time, and money to our publication? This resolution should be seen more as a partial solution to a problem brought up by our ambitions. In our first long term planning retreat, we agreed to aim for a membership of 1000 within the next five years. Some comrades have brought up fears that are, broadly, about the quality of that new mass membership. What if they are liberals, or reactionaries? What if these members do not aid in the capacity of the chapter, and instead stay as ‘paper members’? I want to cast the first problem wholly away. I do not have the politics I had when I joined DSA. In fact, the politics I have now did not exist when I joined DSA, but instead emerged from the interaction of hundreds of people with practical organizing . That is the experience of so many comrades in our organization, and I see no reason that it will cease being the case in the future. What we should worry about, more than what the new members call themselves the moment they join, is: what will we give them to do ? When I joined ROC DSA, the organization was two years old and we were just figuring ourselves out. What kind of work would we do, what were the boundaries of our politics, why are we even doing anything we did? There was a degree of pressure then, in 2017-2020, for us to become similar to the other left wing organizations around us at the time. Groups like Metro Justice dwarfed us, and had a clear eyed focus on basebuilding, mobilizing, and lobbying towards the end of getting radical legislation passed. Other organizations were even more focused on lobbying. A criticism I had of this approach is that lobbying focuses us on very specific people – it requires getting enough members who have free time, specialized skills, and the drive to get in a bus at 5AM on a weekday to go to Albany and pressure our electeds to little effect. I believed that we needed, instead, something that could produce a mass politics. But I have a self-criticism. Far too often, the answer I and our chapter had to a new member asking “what do I do about the growth of fascism in the US?” is to say “clear a weekday, you’re going to be in a meeting deciding what we’ll do!”. Our meetings have gotten better, and as a whole we are far better at meeting discipline than we were in 2023 (when, during the primary season, we had more meetings than days in the month). But those criticisms I had of lobbying – that it requires people with free time, specialized skills, and the drive to keep going without clear wins – all apply to meetings-as-praxis. They also require specialized skills, they all require drive, and in fact they require more of our free time. Now, I am not saying that meetings are bad, and I am very much not saying that we should stop deliberating. But if meetings are for the purpose of making decisions about the work we are doing, far too often the leadership work of filtering day to day activities into something people can meaningfully make a decision on, and making decisions into tasks that are assigned and then followed up on, is left to the meeting, and so meetings become multiple people deciding on the logistics of something that one person should be figuring out, rather than thinking about the broader direction we are going in. If we are going to be an organization of thousands of members, that has hundreds of active members, then we will need to give those members something they can meaningfully do. For the most active, that may look like meetings and making dozens upon dozens of decisions about the tactics and logistics of the chapter. Ideally, general meetings would be a place where all the decisions are filtered to a place where membership can meaningfully choose strategic directions. But for many, many members, their engagement will look like something smaller. Anyone who’s been to a labor training will have seen this graphic: The ‘core’ for us is leadership, the hyper-engaged, people who know a bunch that’s going on and who have a high level of time commitment to the chapter. Outside of that is activists, people who are engaged but perhaps not consistent, who maybe don’t have a fully formed idea of what they want to do with the chapter. Further outside are supporters (who maybe show up to a meeting every so often) and the disengaged (who are, at best, paper members). Something that was brought up to me the first time I was shown this has stuck with me since: that the best way to get a member to move deeper into the bullseye is to get them to feel they are representing the organization in some way. They get the ‘big sibling’ educational effect, where older siblings who are forced to teach their younger siblings end up reinforcing their grasp of the material by expressing the lesson in their own words. So a disengaged member, who is expressing socialist ideas to their friends, is finding their own way to articulate them. A supporter who tables for us ends up having dozens of conversations where they’re speaking on behalf of all of us, and it gives them a better sense of what they want from this organization and how they can help us. This could be an argument for any clearly defined, front facing set of tasks, and I want to be clear I support us engaging in all of them more. City Vitality has done very well for its clear outward facing task. But this resolution centers Red Star, and gives whatever priority campaign we have reserved column space, for a reason. For the development of our chapter’s rich inner life, we are not yet, as a chapter, in the habit of explaining our political perspective externally. We are good at slogans, we are good at developing conversations internal to the chapter, we are getting better at developing campaigns towards the political ends we’ve decided on, but when it comes to arguing our beliefs in depth, that is a skill that many members have, but which we do not have as an organization. When our leaders in the Steering Committee attended a pretty hostile interview on WXXI the other month, there were several times they seemed stumped. I do not think this is a failing of these comrades, it is a failing of a chapter culture which hasn’t developed the habit of putting out clear socialist analysis. This is understandable as we’ve worked to build, from the ground up, a socialist organization in this city. But just like meeting centricity, it is not fitted to a truly mass politics. We need to get better at creating smaller, outward-facing, manageable tasks if we want to become a truly mass organization. We can do that without giving up the rich internal life we have built for ourselves in ROC DSA. City Vitality’s outreach walks and External Organizings’ tablings are two examples, but we need more, easily manageable tasks, for the organization to thrive. And for us to win, in our long term goal of the working class governing society, we need to get far more comfortable with articulating ourselves to it. People are excited, desperate, to do something in this moment. We need something to say, and something to do. The post On Clear Tasks and Meetings first appeared on Rochester Red Star .
